prize_parts.citation: For the development of base editing, in which a deaminase tethered to a Cas9 nickase chemically converts single DNA bases at programmed sites in living cells without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: base editing, credited to Liu, Komor and Gaudelli. Round 1 left it the only configuration with more than one explicit supporter (Chabes, Zou and me), and the chair's point that support is a plurality and not a majority is correct, so I rest the case on the science. The chemical result is specific. A cytidine deaminase, and for the adenine editor a TadA evolved to act on DNA where no natural enzyme does, is fused to a nickase, so one base is converted in place and the cell's own repair fixes the change. The product is a defined single-nucleotide transition verified at nucleotide resolution, reproduced by many laboratories, and used in first clinical studies. The chair asked whether this is a sufficient increment over 2020. I think the 2020 citation honoured programmable cleavage of DNA and base editing is chemistry done without cleavage, so a citation worded around deamination at a programmed site credits something the 2020 text did not. The attribution follows the sequence of work: Komor and Liu for the cytosine editor, Gaudelli and Liu for the evolved adenine editor.
statement.case_against: The increment over 2020 is a judgement, not a measurement, and a colleague may still read base editing as a downstream application of a platform already honoured. It is the youngest candidacy (2016-2017), with a short clinical record and open questions on off-target deamination, bystander editing and delivery. Kondo and Nishida's Target-AID is an independent cytidine deaminase fusion, and the three-person limit excludes them. I also note that Somfai and Sparr remain unconvinced, so this is not a settled majority position and I will not treat it as one.

responses.point: Linke asks what a base-editing citation would credit that the CRISPR citation did not, and doubts the full trio since Liu was the intellectual driver.
responses.response: The 2020 text concerns guided cleavage of DNA. The base-editing citation should be worded around chemical conversion of one base, deamination at a programmed position, with no double-strand break. That is a different reaction with a different outcome, and the evolved adenine deaminase has no natural counterpart. On names, I accept that Liu led both programmes. Still, Komor made the first cytosine editor and Gaudelli carried out the directed evolution of the DNA adenine deaminase, which is the hardest chemical step. The record I can see supports crediting the named lead inventors, so I keep three. I also hold my round-1 difficulty with your nanopore configuration: it needs a cut of five claimants to three, and every cut drops someone whose step was necessary.

responses.point: Somfai asks what is new chemically beyond the fusion concept, and notes the 2020 prize already recognised programmable targeting.
responses.response: Targeting was recognised in 2020, and I do not dispute that. What is new is the chemical event placed under that targeting: in situ deamination of a base in genomic DNA, followed by exploitation of mismatch repair. For the adenine editor, no enzyme existed that deaminates adenine in DNA, so TadA had to be evolved from an RNA-acting enzyme. That is enzyme engineering in the service of a new reaction, not only a fusion. I still regard Buchwald-Hartwig as a mature, cleanly attributed candidacy, but your own reservation about the 2010 cross-coupling prize is the same type of increment question, and I judge the new-function argument stronger for base editing.

responses.point: Sparr puts base editing first among her alternatives but does not think it clearly outranks ionizable lipid nanoparticles on maturity.
responses.response: I accept that delivery chemistry has reached far more patients, and the maturity gap is real. My difficulty with B017 remains attribution: after your own revision to a Vancouver trio, Anderson, Langer and MacLachlan are excluded with real claims, and the 2023 Medicine prize sits close to it. For base editing the three names track the actual steps of the work. Maturity is the right criterion to weigh, but I give it less weight than a clean credit when the field is already producing clinical data.

responses.point: Aqvist would move base editing up if priority is shown to be clean, and notes a prize might have to absorb prime editing for Liu.
responses.response: Priority is not fully clean for the cytosine editor, because Target-AID is independent, and I will not claim otherwise. It is narrower than it looks: Target-AID is a cytidine deaminase fusion, while the adenine editor has no independent parallel, and the citation can be worded around base editing as a class. Prime editing is later and clinically thinner, so I would keep it out of this citation. Your phase-separation case is strong on quantitative physics, and I keep it as an alternative, but the live in vivo question you raise yourself makes a precise citation harder than the one for base editing.

responses.point: Zou notes that a Liu-only prize is defensible, that trainee credit is a judgement call, and wants the citation explicit about deamination without cleavage.
responses.response: I agree on the citation wording and have adopted it. On Liu alone, I considered it, but a one-person prize would misdescribe where the cytosine and adenine editors were first made, and Chabes made the same argument. I do not change to a Liu-only configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges base editing a sufficient increment over the 2020 prize, given that the citation is worded around chemical conversion without cleavage.
Whether Kondo and Nishida need to be credited, which would force a different three-name cut.
How the expert reports weigh the short clinical record and unresolved off-target and bystander questions.
Whether support will consolidate to five votes, or whether more mature candidacies such as B068 or B032 draw late support.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate or credited name. Xiaodong Zou is my Stockholm University colleague, which is not a tie to any candidate. As Secretary I hold a procedural role only, and I have no change to my disclosure from round 1.
